messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 20
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Stalking
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mele was 20, a first-year auditor living alone and trying to establish herself in a demanding office where long hours and careful attention were prized. The trauma began not as a single dramatic assault but as a pattern that gradually closed around her. A man she had briefly spoken to several times near her apartment and once outside the downtown building where she worked began appearing in places that should have been unrelated: across the street from her bus stop in the morning, near the coffee shop beneath her office, outside the grocery store she used after work. At first she told herself she might be imagining it, but the repetition stripped that explanation away. He would stand still and watch her. Once, as she left work after staying late to finish audit documentation, she saw him half-hidden by a parked car and felt the instant, sick certainty that he knew her routines better than she did. After that, ordinary parts of the city—an elevator opening into the lobby, footsteps behind her on the sidewalk, someone lingering too long near the entrance of her building—no longer felt neutral. They felt like proof that nowhere was protected.

In the weeks that followed, Mele came to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous and that safety depended on never relaxing. What frightened her most was not only that he had followed her, but what it seemed to reveal: that anyone could watch, wait, and intrude without warning. She became convinced she had to be on guard all the time. Walking to work, she scanned reflections in windows and checked who was behind her. At the office, where part of her job involved moving between conference rooms and records areas, she kept track of exits and noticed every unfamiliar face in the reception area. Even when she was seated at her desk reviewing spreadsheets, some part of her attention stayed fixed on whether someone might be outside the glass doors. Alongside that vigilance, her view of her future darkened. She had started adulthood expecting independence and possibility; now she said it felt as if her life had been destroyed by what happened, as though the ordinary confidence of being young and building a career had been taken from her and not returned.

Those beliefs began to shape how she lived. Because she was certain danger was everywhere and that any lapse could invite more harm, she started avoiding going out except when it seemed absolutely necessary. She took the most direct route between work and home and cut out errands that were not essential. If coworkers invited her to get dinner after a late close or celebrate the end of a busy week, she declined, telling herself that being out longer only increased the chances of being seen, followed, or trapped. The same conviction drained the meaning from anything that might have brought relief. Situations that could make her feel happy or hopeful began to feel almost intolerable, not because she had lost the capacity for pleasure entirely, but because allowing herself to enjoy them seemed unsafe and naive. If she accepted a social invitation or let herself look forward to a weekend plan, she felt she was forgetting the reality she now believed governed the world. In that sense, avoiding positive moments became part of staying alert.

Over time, her appraisals turned inward as well. Mele had come to believe that what had happened had ruined her life, and from there it was a short step to feeling that she herself should suffer for it. She would tell herself she deserved to suffer because of what happened, as though any comfort or ease would be undeserved. When she spent another evening alone in her apartment after work, eating something quick and ignoring messages from friends, there was a harsh logic to it in her mind: if the world was dangerous and her life already wrecked, then denying herself anything enjoyable felt fitting, almost morally required. The more she thought this way, the smaller her life became. Her work remained intact on paper, but colleagues had noticed she never joined group lunches and always left with visible tension, checking the street before stepping outside. She was still performing, but at the cost of constant strain and increasing isolation.

By the time she sought help, Mele was exhausted by the effort of maintaining this guarded life. What finally pushed her into treatment was not a new stalking incident but the recognition that she was structuring every day around threat and deprivation. She could see how little remained beyond work and vigilance. She was most afraid that this was permanent—that she would always live as if watched, always deny herself ordinary happiness, and never again feel that the world contained any safe place for her. At the same time, a small part of her hoped that if someone understood how completely this fear had reorganized her life, she might not have to keep punishing herself just to feel prepared.
